Before the motion is put, I should like to know if members of parliament who have grievances on behalf of returned men will have an opportunity of submitting their cases to the committee in order to try to get some help for these men. It seems that the pension commission is helpless, and I can say the same thing for the commission on allowances. I have every sympathy for the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe). He is an able gentleman, and a personal friend of mine. The members of the pension commission, and the members of the commission for allowances, are procrastinating. It is useless to argue the case of any soldier with them. I have some pitiful cases, and it is impossible to reach the heart of these commission members in discussing these problems which are of vital importance to the soldiers and their families.
Will the members of the house who do not belong to the committee have an opportunity of appearing before the committee with these files? Some of them are voluminous.
The pension commission seems to take it for granted that in some cases the soldiers suffered from disabilities before enlistment. I have one case in particular in which I was told the soldier was suffering from heart trouble before his enlistment, and that his five years of active military service had not increased his disability. I wrote to the department that it was absurd, and I was informed a month later that he was not suffering from heart trouble. This was an example.
Another case is that of a soldier, number 597, of the first war. He was in service during the whole of the war. He was overseas for at least four years, if not five. He was a big fellow, with the appearance of a strong man. I could not get anything for him except some treatment at the hospital which did him no good. He enlisted again in the second war, and it is impossible to get a pension for him. There are other cases where soldiers have a small pension, and there is the allowance board, which does nothing to give them an opportunity to live as decent men are supposed to live.
I have many cases which I could cite. The doctors are all fools except perhaps one or two. I keep in reserve some cases of murder which I have already mentioned in the house-murder by the army doctors of the province of Ontario and of the province of Quebec. There was another one who escaped in the province of New Brunswick. He had protection from the high-ranking people in the medical service of the army. Some army doctors are good. Some others are rotten. This is one of the reasons why I object so greatly to a program of health insurance, because those army doctors will have some kind of preference. I think of the district medical officer at Montreal. Who is the district medical officer at Montreal? He is a complete failure with regard to medical qualifications. What is his record as a medical officer? He was overseas on a Cook's tour for a month or two, and he was to come to Ottawa. I strongly protested at the time to the then hon. member for Halifax, Mr. Macdonald-who was the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence- and to Walter Tucker, who helped me a great deal when he was parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs.
I am fighting the case of the soldiers who cannot expect any justice from the pension

Reports of Committees commission or from the allowance board. One day I decided to send a motion to the Clerk of the House, but unf ortunately it was not signed, and according to the rules it did not appear on the order paper. The motion called for the abolition of the pension commission and the allowance board. So long as the soldiers get no benefits from these boards, what is the use of paying big salaries to these men who give relief by a dropper to the soldier?
I will ask the minister to consider the remarks I have made in the friendliest spirit to him, but I have not the same spirit with regard to these boards and commissions. They are there to earn a big salary and to do nothing. They are all alike, from Melville down. The other day when I saw him, with all his decorations, I thought of the poor devils who have such a great struggle and who cannot get any help. We have to write and write again, but we never receive a decent answer from the silly and selfish bureaucrats. I hope that there will be reform in due course and that the members who sit on the committee will be ready to defend the case of the soldier instead of lying down before such awful bureaucrats.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO DEFERMENT OF DEPRECIATION FOR INCOME TAX PURPOSES

speechtext: On the order for motions:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO DEFERMENT OF DEPRECIATION FOR INCOME TAX PURPOSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his discustMr Pouliot.]
sion of the budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) stated that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would make a statement on deferred capital cost allowances, and at the conclusion of his budget speech the minister tabled a copy of order in council P.C. 1778, dated April 10, 1951, which altered the regulations affecting capital cost allowances under the Income Tax Act.
The purposes of these changes in the regulations is to defer capital cost allowances for a period of three years beyond the date of acquisition; that is a total of four years, except in certain specified cases. As the Minister of Finance explained:
What we need is a stiff financial deterrent that will affect particularly the businessman who is considering the kind of investment which is attractive, not because of its long-term soundness but because it can be written off out of the expected high profits of the next few years, at a time when he expects the rate of corporate income tax to be abnormally high.
To provide this deterrent it is proposed to defer for a period of four years the right to charge depreciation on all capital assets acquired after April 10, 1951, excepting certain classes of assets defined in the regulations and certain additional kinds of assets when certified as eligible by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Under the proposal, the right to charge depreciation as an expense is deferred, not cancelled or even diminished. For example, $10,000 of ineligible assets acquired after April 10, 1951, will earn no depreciation for tax purposes during the next four years; but in 1955 it can be transferred by the depreciable asset account at its full original cost. If it is a type of asset that can be written off in say ten years, it will be written off in 1955 to 1964 instead of in 1951 to 1960.
The deterrent will particularly affect the businessman whose decision to make a capital expenditure is strongly influenced by the expectation that he can write off a large fraction of his cost at a time when both profits and tax rates are abnormally high, particularly if it is a kind of investment with uncertain profit-making possibilities six or eight years hence. In other words it will compel the businessman to give primary attention to the long-term prospects of proposed capital expenditures, and, if outside financial participation is required, lenders will also take this view.
There will, therefore, be a stiff deterrent on projects of uncertain long-run value and also on capital expenditures on frills, gadgets and generally "dressing up" offices, stores and buildings. This deterrent should reduce the competitive scramble for scarce materials and equipment and thus place less strain on direct controls. Such materials and equipment will tend to go to those who can make the best long-term use of them. Bidders who are anticipating short-run quick profits will tend to withdraw from the market.
One further advantage is that the government will not be telling anyone that he cannot do this or that. What will happen is that a financial penalty will be put, in the short run, on those who go ahead with less essential expenditures.
These revised depreciation regulations will go into effect immediately and will apply to all capital assets acquired after April 10, 1951.
That is the end of the quotation from the budget speech.

Current capital cost allowances will continue to be available on all property acquired up to and including April 10, 1951. Determination of the date of acquisition will be made by the Department of National Revenue in accordance with its usual practice in such cases.
With respect to property acquired after April 10, 1951, current capital cost allowances will be allowed to individual farmers, fishermen and professional men. Current allowances will also continue to be available to all taxpayers where the property acquired falls into any of the following categories set forth in schedule B of the income tax regulations:
Class 1. This class covers such properties as bridges, canals, culverts, dams, et cetera.
Class 2. This class covers such properties as pipe lines and certain plant connected with the production or distribution of electrical energy, gas and water.
Class 4. This class covers properties of a railway system, a telegraph or telephone system and a tramway or trolley bus system.
Class 9. This class covers such properties as radar equipment and radio transmission equipment.
Class 10. This class covers automotive equipment, gas or oil well equipment, mining machinery equipment and some other items.
Class 12. This class covers certain articles that have a limited life and can be depreciated entirely within a year.
Class 14. This class covers certain patents, franchises, concessions and licences.
As I have said properties which fall into any of the foregoing classes can be depreciated in the normal way and will not be subject to certification by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Similarly, current capital cost allowances will be available without certification with respect to all residential properties, that is, houses and apartment blocks, and with respect to all properties which replace those that have been destroyed by fire, flood, wind, lightning or other act of God.
I now come to those properties acquired after April 10, 1951, which will be eligible for current capital cost allowances only if a certificate is issued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. These fall into two categories: (1) a property acquired for the fulfilment of a defence contract or subcontract or for a purpose which contributes to the defence of Canada; (2) a property acquired by a taxpayer for carrying on certain businesses.
Let me deal first with properties which are acquired for defence purposes. Hon. members will, I think, readily understand the reason
Capital Cost Allowances for this provision. The government does not wish to discourage in any way capital expenditures which will enable Canadian industry to build up its productive facilities to meet Canada's defence needs. Moreover in some cases the investment may have a use limited to the defence period, and it would be inequitable to defer capital cost allowances for four years.
Taxpayers who have defence contracts and who find it necessary to acquire properties in order to fulfil defence contracts or subcontracts should apply to the capital cost allowances division of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the necessary forms and information. Before a certificate is granted, it will be necessary for the taxpayer to give evidence that the defence contract cannot be fulfilled unless the property in question is acquired.
Certificates may also be issued with respect to properties acquired by the taxpayer which in the opinion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce contribute to the defence of Canada. This provision is included to enable the minister to give a certificate for projects which, though not undertaken for the fulfilment or specific defence contracts or subcontracts, are nevertheless important as a means of increasing supplies of some basic material or commodity or of supplying some essential service. Such certificates will be issued only in exceptional cases.
In the second category is a group of basic industries listed in the order in council. Broadly, the industries covered include primary industries, industries engaged in the processing, including smelting and refining, of raw materials, and enterprises providing a utility or hospital service.
The policy in this category will be to issue certificates of eligibility for properties acquired by the taxpayer that are necessary to the carrying on of these businesses. Certificates will not be issued, however, if the property acquired is primarily used for the purpose of hotel or office use, commercial service, finance, wholesale trade, retail trade or renting for other than residential habitation.
Taxpayers who fall into the list of businesses included in this second category should apply to the capital cost allowances division of the Department of Trade and Commerce for forms and other information.
Before concluding this statement I should like to add just one comment, and that is that in administering these regulations neither the Department of Trade and Commerce nor any other department of government is making a decision as to whether or not any particular capital expenditure should be made.

Aeronautics Act
That is for the taxpayer to decide. As my colleague the Minister of Finance said, " . . . the government will not be telling anyone that he cannot do this or that."
These regulations are another aspect of the government's policy to combat inflation. They are designed to reduce the competition for scarce materials and equipment, and thus to place less strain on direct controls.

subtopic: REPORTED REQUEST OF HOLLINGER COMPANY FOR PERMISSION TO EMPLOY DISPLACED PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should
Supply-Transport
like to give the answer to a question asked yesterday on the orders of the day by the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais).
(Translation):
The hon. member inquired whether the Hollinger North Shore Company requested that refugees be admitted to Canada for employment in its plants.
I must inform the hon. member that the Department of Labour received no such request, nor does anything indicate that this company intends to place any request for the admission of non-Canadian workers. If, perchance, any such request were made, it would first, like any other application of this nature, be submitted to the offices of the national employment service in the district concerned, and throughout the country if necessary, to make sure that no workers are available locally to fill the jobs. Only after those usual precautions had been taken could a request of this nature be given attention and favourable consideration.
(Text):

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Dion in the chair.
471. Departmental administration, $1,199,818.

I should like to say a few words about the report of the royal commission on transportation, which was discussed to some extent the other evening.
I think that the members of the board, the Hon. W. F. A. Turgeon, Dr. H. F. Angus and Dr. H. A. Innis, did a very fine job indeed for Canada when they made this inquiry and wrote their report. The report to a very large extent vindicates the position taken in this house by those of us who criticized some of the decisions of the board of transport commissioners, and also vindicates the attitude of the seven provinces which objected to those decisions and asked for the establishment of a royal commission of inquiry.
With some opinions in the report I find myself in disagreement, but they are minor considerations compared with the major recommendations of the report. I noted with a good deal of interest that the commission referred to the request which has been made from various quarters in the country for legislation which would prevent a recurrence of the regrettable dispute and the regrettable strike which occurred last summer. I noted with considerable interest that the royal commission recommended that no special legislation should be passed for the handling of railway disputes and the prevention of strikes or lockouts. It went on to

Supply-Transport
say that legislation of that kind would be highly provocative and in practice ineffective -in other words, that we should continue the traditional method enjoyed by labour and management through the years, namely, collective bargaining.
Some of us who took that view last year were subjected to considerable criticism here and there across the country. Indeed, those of us who had the temerity to say that, after the long months of negotiation which ended in failure to achieve a settlement, the railway unions were justified in the regrettable action they then took, can find, I think, both in the report of the royal commission and in the report of the special commissioner or arbitrator who dealt with that railway dispute, some consolation for the, in some respects, abusive remarks directed toward us last August and September.
So as to link the matter up, I wish to place on record a paragraph of some significance in Mr. Justice Kellock's report:
By September 1, 1950, the wage rate-cost ot living relationship of the railway worker had deteriorated from the 1948 level to such an extent that 10 2 cents per hour was then required to restore that relationship.
In other words the seven cents asked for- by the railway unions-was already exceeded by 3-2 cents.
And this margin, it would appear, will likely continue to be augmented.
That margin of course has continued to be augmented. It is indeed regrettable that strikes have to occur; but at the same time, when we find the justification outlined in the report of the arbitrator in the railway dispute, it can readily be seen why such action becomes necessary. I am glad to note the royal commission states that we should continue to rely upon the traditional methods of collective bargaining and not upon legislation referring particularly to employees of such public services as the railway.
I agree with the commission that it is unfortunate that railway freight rates for quite a number of years now have been a matter of public controversy, and unless action is taken, in some respects along the lines suggested in the report of the royal commission, we shall continue for a long time to come to have these regrettable discussions and disputes, and these feelings of justifiable dissatisfaction in various parts of the country. There will also be the feeling, as there has been in that part of Canada which has been my home for a good many years, including the constituency I represent, that there has been both unjust treatment and unjust discrimination against large sections of the country, both the far east and the far west.

In justification of the criticism we have made in the house from time to time I would point out that the royal commission indulges in some criticism of the board's decisions since world war II. Those are decisions we have criticized adversely and at times severely in the house. The report says:
The board seems to have treated the application purely from the revenue point of view and without considering the ability of different commodities to bear the increase.
I think that has very largely been the bone of contention. Incidentally it contrasts the attitude of our board of transport commissioners with that of the interstate commerce commission in the United States, pointing out that the American board, which has similar functions, did take into consideration some factors other than purely revenue factors, and that in their decisions there had been numerous exemptions from the horizontal increase right across the board about which we have complained in this country.
Quite properly in this connection the royal commission points out that special consideration must be given, both by the parliament of Canada and by any authority set up by parliament, to the long haul traffic, and particularly to the traffic in primary commodities. We have long argued in the house that the railways should not be considered purely from the point of view of revenue-producing institutions or organizations. The Canadian Pacific railway in particular was built to cement confederation. Indeed, one of the fundamental factors in the confederation agreement, particularly with British Columbia, was that a railway would be built to unite the far western province of British Columbia with the central and eastern provinces of the new Canada. It was on that consideration that British Columbia entered confederation. In other words, the railway was the bond of steel that joined the country together, considered not from a revenue-producing or economic standpoint only, but also as a political factor in the uniting of this great country we now know as Canada.
One can understand that the railways themselves are loath to approach the problem from the point of view I have just indicated. The royal commissioners pointed out -and I say the House of Commons should see that the suggestion is carried out-that the board of transport commissioners must approach the problem from what, for the want of a better term, I shall describe as the political point of view, or the point of view of the political welfare of the entire Dominion of Canada.
Then in connection with rate structure they say, as we have said in the house on

many occasions, that we must have some equalization of treatment in the matter of freight rates. Indeed, it would appear that from the evidence given before the royal commission they came to the conclusion that that point of view was now generally accepted in all parts of Canada. In other words they felt that our friends in eastern Canada now recognize, with the rest of us, that these injustices and discriminations must be removed, and that there must be more equality in the rate structure of our country than we have had up to the present time. Therefore I am much in agreement with that part of the report. I think the recommendation as to the treatment of rates across the country is based on sound reasoning.
The commission point out that British Columbia in some respects enjoys a competitive rate because of the water haul by the Panama canal, but that certain cities in western Canada, particularly Edmonton and Calgary, have been discriminated against. They show that the rate on canned goods from eastern Canada to Vancouver is $1.40 per hundred pounds, because of the competition, as compared with a rate of $2.65 to Calgary or Edmonton. They recommend that a new system of rating should be adopted which would bring the rate to the Alberta cities down to $1.87 per hundred pounds. They recommend that the rates to intermediate points between the east and British Columbia should never be more than one-third greater than the transcontinental rates to or from the Pacific coast. It seems to me that that is one of the wisest and fairest recommendations in this report.
At least it is closer to reason.

It is getting closer to what we should have in the way of a rate structure. It does tend to remove at least some of the injustices that are found in the present rate structure. What we need is a rate structure that will treat all citizens of Canada, wherever they may live, as justly as it is possible to do under prevailing conditions.
I am not going into a discussion of competitive rates generally, or the proposals in the report of the commission in regard to them. I have no doubt that soon or later the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier)-at least I hope so-will be bringing down legislation to implement some of the good recommendations in this report.
I notice that the commission does not recommend the public ownership of the Canadian Pacific railway. Some time ago we urged in this house that public ownership of the Canadian Pacific railway should be considi-
Supply-Transport
ered. During the war many of the securities issued by the Canadian Pacific, and indeed many of its shares, were held in the United Kingdom. Under wartime legislation in Great Britain those securities and shares were picked up by the government and marketed in order to get dollar exchange.
We were most anxious, as we are still, that the Canadian Pacific railway shall not pass into the control of the nationals of even the friendliest of foreign countries. That kind of thing has been going on. I still think that when we had the opportunity we would have been wise to ensure to the Canadian people the ownership of this great transportation facility. However, that was not done, and the report of the royal commission does not recommend that it should be done now. Indeed, it rejected the plea that it should be done.
May I just note in passing that the plea for the public ownership of the Canadian Pacific railway came from Prince Edward Island1. That province produced some strong arguments as to why this railway should be publicly owned. My own province of Saskatchewan did not make a representation in the same sense as the Liberal government of Prince Edward Island.
Prince Edward Island is the only province through which the Canadian Pacific does not run.

That is right. While I have been criticized for saying it, I repeat that if and1 when this railway does come under the ownership of the people of Canada, as I believe it will ultimately, personally I would not be in favour of creating a single authority for the operation and amalgamation of the two great railroad systems. I believe that they should be competing in giving service with one another, just as it has been found advisable in the United Kingdom, and in some other countries where industries of the same type are publicly owned, to have separate management and administration, in order that one unit of the industry in one area may become a yardstick for another unit of the same industry in another area. I wanted to refer to that because it is something I have talked about in this house for a very long time.
The commission recommends an amendment to the Railway Act to empower the board and direct it to maintain a revised statistical procedure so designed as to provide the requisite data for the purposes of its duties. During the course of the presentations by the various provinces to the board of transport commissioners I was told that there was a sad lack of statistical material available, and

Supply-Transport
that they had neither the staff nor the facilities to do the job they were expected to do under the legislation. I was told that by counsel who appeared before the commission, and particularly by some of the expert accountants who were engaged in the presentation of the pleas of the various provinces before the board of transport commissioners. I notice that the royal commission directs the attention of the house and the minister to the necessity of an amendment to the Railway Act to empower and direct the board to have the facilities available to enable them to do the kind of statistical job that is necessary in connection with problems of this kind.
It is noteworthy that two of the recommendations in the report are of great interest to two particular parts of Canada, because there is legislation dealing with both of them. No one wishes to disturb the maritime freight rates structure; and by the same token I was pleased indeed to see, in spite of representations by the railways, that the royal commission recommends no interference with the Crowsnest pass rates. We in western Canada regard the Crowsnest pass agreement as one of the agreements vital to the economic welfare of our part of Canada and indeed all Canada. We feel that we have paid in full for the right which is embedded in that agreement and in the validating legislation of this House of Commons. Some of us can remember very distinctly the attempts that were made after world war I to set aside the Crowsnest pass agreement. We remember the long struggle, lasting until 1925, to prevent any interference with that agreement; and we regretted and still regret that we lost some advantages when the legislation was amended, I think in 1925 or thereabouts. But as it remains today it is of such vital importance to western Canada that I am delighted indeed to see that the royal commission recommended that the Crowsnest pass agreement should remain under the control of parliament and not be turned back to the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners, as the railways requested should be done.
I was also pleased to see that the royal commission took up the argument which is sometimes advanced that these Crowsnest rates inflict some burden upon the rest of Canada. The commission did not substantiate that contention. Indeed they pointed out that other parts of the country enjoyed certain advantages which quite offset any advantages given under the Crowsnest agreement. Consequently they recommended that these rates should not be made to bear any part of general freight rate increases. As I say, we are pleased indeed that the royal commission

confirmed the point of view many hon. members from western Canada, regardless of political affiliation, have advanced1 in this house from time to time.
I think one of the most interesting sections in the report is that which deals with the unproductive haul across northern and1 western Ontario, between Sudbury and Fort William. In that connection they have a proposal which I think this house would be well advised to consider very carefully, because it is the most constructive proposal I have seen along these lines during the years I have been in parliament or since this matter has been under discussion. They propose that this unproductive area from Sudbury to Fort William be considered on exactly the same basis as the canal system of Canada, which joins the great lakes and is the responsibility of all Canada. They propose that this long haul should be considered in exactly the same light, and that the annual maintenance costs-they make it clear that they are not talking about the operating costs-of that part of our railway system should be borne entirely by the federal government. They estimate that this would relieve the freight rate structure to the extent of something like $7 million annually, and they anticipate that this would be an effective measure of relief in the case of westbound traffic passing over this area which they call the bridge between east and west. I think that proposition would be fair to the railways and beneficial to all Canada. I believe it should be carefully considered and, if that consideration is favourable, approved by this house.
As I said before the report does not recommend any other legislation regarding railway disputes, strikes, lockouts, and so on. Another part of the report which I think should be carefully considered deals with the methods suggested for meeting the growing trucking competition. As a matter of fact I think everyone realizes that the truck is here to stay, and that it can perform a very useful function within our transportation system. While local trucking is under provincial control, there is no doubt that the house and the government, through legislation, cam exercise some control over interprovincial and international trucking. What seems to be happening is that am many instances the lighter, more profitable traffic that might have been hauled by the railways has been picked up by the trucking and bus companies. As a result the railways have been denied a large and profitable traffic they might otherwise have had. If this continues without consideration and without perhaps some supervision, more and more we are going to find the railways left with coal, lumber, wheat and other heavy

commodities, with the lighter and more profitable traffic handled1 almost exclusively by trucks and busses. I am not suggesting by any means the elimination of the trucking industry. As I said, I believe it performs a very useful function within our transportation system. I am suggesting, however, that the time has come when the minister and this house should consider the best ways and means of treating the trucking industry fairly and at the same time regulating it so it will be supplementary or complementary, whichever expression you like better, to the railway transportation system which must always be, within foreseeable time, the basic transportation system of this country, just as the fathers of confederation regarded it when confederation was achieved.
There are many other important matters dealt with in the report. I notice that the commission recommends the establishment of one central board to supervise our entire transportation system instead of the board of transport commissioners, the air transport board, and the Canadian maritime commission. That is one board instead of three. They say such a board would be able to undertake the kind of co-ordinated control that in these days is essential to the efficiency and welfare of the various groups and interests engaged1 in transportation, and for the protection of the public of Canada.
There is not a great deal more that I wish to say at this point. I do think that the minister will find he has a considerable amount of support in this house for the main recommendations made by the royal commission. If I may speak personally, I believe that the time has arrived when the recommendation for a national transportation commission, dealing with all forms of transportation which could come properly within the jurisdiction of such a commission, should be carefully considered by the minister and by the government. As the minister knows, I have held that view for a long time. The more I study the railway problem in Canada, the more I have been convinced that if we are going to have the kind of rate structure that will be satisfactory to all Canada, even if we have these changes that are recommended by the royal commission, if we are going to maintain our basic transportation system, then we have to view the transportation problem not from the railways' standpoint, not from the viewpoint of the trucking industry or the aeroplanes or the ships or whatever you have, but from the point of view of the entire industry and the economic effect of that industry on the welfare of Canada. When I say "welfare of Canada", we have now of course to consider also the interests of Newfoundland, as well as the 80709-124
Supply-Transport
interests of the nine provinces who were interested in this problem when it came before the house so acutely two or three years ago.
I want to say again that I believe the royal commission did ia splendid job for Canada. The commission members are to be congratulated. The main recommendations of the report I believe are of such a nature that this house would be well advised to give early consideration to them, and to enacting legislation to bring into effect, as soon as we can, those that we feel are in the interests of Canada.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Would the hon. member care to tell the house exactly how he would propose to manage the railroads, if both railroads were owned by the federal government? Would he cut out duplicate services?

Mr. Chairman, you will note that in discussing this several years ago I said that ownership of the Canadian Pacific might come to us if we acquired its securities then held in the United Kingdom instead of allowing them to pass into the hands of citizens of the United States, and that then we would have to consider that problem. I say I believe the day will yet come when the railways will be nationally owned. Economic circumstances will ultimately force that on the people of Canada, because sooner or later the people of Canada will decide that they should not subsidize a private railway company.
I said that when that is done I personally would not be in favour, as I see it now at least, of setting up one great corporation to operate the railways as one great system. The recommendation of the commission is to set up a controlling body over these various phases of transportation. I would say that, at least until that has been tried, no further step might be necessary.
The hon. member asked me how one would administer the two railways. I would say, keep each under an administration somewhat similar to the administration you have today, that is separate administrations answerable, as is the Canadian National, for their operations to a committee of parliament. I have forgotten the last question I was asked.

If the two railways were
united it would appear that, in the interests of economy, all duplicate services should be discontinued.

I did not suggest the uniting of the two railways. As a matter of fact,

Supply-Transport
when you speak about duplication of service, let us bear in mind that the parliament of Canada granted charters to these railroads to build where they are today. Along these routes that were granted, the people built towns and villages. I believe that in any consideration of the railway problem the interests of these towns and villages must be of primary consideration to us. To take up lines through certain territories because they are duplicated would create hardship on many hundreds of people. This parliament or provincial legislatures allowed the railways to go there, the duplication occurred, and this encouraged the building of towns and villages along those routes. We must not penalize the people who settled those parts of the country in good faith.

I should like to say a few words on this report, because in the past I have had something to say about transportation. I believe it can be fairly said that the report has covered a large field, and that the members of the commission have done an excellent job. They have spent a good deal of time on it, I think in all about two years. In general the recommendations which the commission have made should commend themselves not only to the members of the house but to the people of Canada as well.
There are some exceptions that I would take to that, however. One of the good things which the report contains, one of the outstanding things, is the recommendation that the government subsidize the bridge between eastern and western Canada. I believe that is designated as the part lying north of the great lakes. We often refer to it as no man's land. I do not see how that problem could be dealt with in any different manner than that recommended by the commission. There is a large area of about four hundred miles between Sudbury and Fort William in which little production is taking place. There has been some improvement in that area due to the building of industries, such as the paper industry, and that will alleviate the distress to some extent. But certainly some assistance must be given to the railways if that large area is not to be considered a hindrance to the progress of western Canada. I believe we can all agree that that is a good recommendation.
The report refers to the amalgamation of the railways, to which the hon. member who preceded me has made some reference. I believe there are not many people in Canada who would support the amalgamation of the railways. The commission definitely recommends against that. My own view is that, while the report says there is not a monopoly existing between the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National Railways, there is what

they term a duopoly. I looked for that word in the dictionary, but I could not find it. The solicitors for the railways gave a definition of it, and it is so close to monopoly there is not much room for argument. I believe the condition which exists with regard to those two railways is quite close enough without any further amalgamation. The commission recommended that the Crowsnest pass rates remain the same and for a good reason, I think, namely that the Crowsnest pass agreement was part of the terms of union of the provinces of Canada. That is necessary in order to maintain that long haul for grain. Incidentally, that reference was made at page 274, where the commission states that it was in the terms of union. It is not necessary to read the citation, but it may be found at page 274.
Then the commissioners make reference to the Maritime Freight Rates Act, which reference is also to be found at page 274, and recommended that it be left as it is. With that recommendation I think we all agree. Then on the same page they make reference to the canal system as follows:
The construction in central Canada of an extensive canal system which became toll free, built at a cost of about $328 million and maintained at government expense.
I think the canal system is necessary to Canada and I am not in disagreement with the report when it suggests that that system be continued. That canal system has been a great advantage to central Canada and I should like to see more rapid progress made with regard to the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway in order to permit ocean-going vessels to go right up to the head of the lakes. That would be a tremendous improvement and advantage having regard to long freight hauls to various parts of this country. But it must not be forgotten that the fact that there was in this country a canal system maintained at the expense of the federal government-and that means maintained at the expense of all of Canada- certainly assisted in the development of central Canada, Ontario and Quebec, in maintaining low rates of transportation.
I have made some reference to that matter at this moment because I want to deal with it at greater length a little later on. I was also interested in and agreed with the recommendation in the report that labour disputes should not be interfered with but that they should be handled under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. I think that is something which should continue to operate as it has in the past. Generally speaking, I think that the Industrial

Relations and Disputes Investigation Act has functioned satisfactorily.
I want to turn my attention now to the chapter which deals with trucking transportation. With some aspects of this report I do not agree, and I think the minister is quite well aware of that fact. I do not agree with them for obvious reasons. While the commission's report itself does not suggest, in so many words, that the federal government take over the control of trucking transportation in Canada, it does that by inference. The trucking industry in this country seems, to me at least, to be of paramount importance.

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I must disagree with the interpretation placed upon the recommendation of the commission. The commission recommends no such thing by inference as the taking over of the trucking industry.

It suggests that the federal government make a further and more extensive investigation into transportation by truck as between provinces. Those are not exactly the words used, but they are so close to it that there is no difference in the meaning at least.
All the commission does is to recommend the amendment of the Railway Act so as t.o cover regulation of international and interprovincial trucking.

If I can just lay my hands on the section here, I will read it to the minister. I will find it a little later on. I cannot just lay my hand on it at the moment. I remember quite well that it was the last sentence of one of the paragraphs. I will run across it in just a moment. I will bring it to the minister's attention later on. As he has said, they do not recommend specifically that the federal government take over control of trucking transport but in my view they were coming fairly close to it, by inference anyway.
The canal system in central Canada has the same effect as the trucking industry would have in western Canada. The commission is explicit about that. They say that because of the canal system in central Canada and the trucking system in that same part of the dominion, there have been much lower traffic rates than there would have been otherwise. They say, in fact, that while the highways are under provincial jurisdiction, trucking transportation has an international effect. At page 275 they have this to say: Under Canada's constitution, control over highway traffic is, in the main, vested in the legislatures of the provinces. The provincial governments have expended large sums of money on road construction
Supply-Transport
and gradually the country is being provided with a network of good roads. Now the federal government is co-operating with the provincial governments in the construction of the "trans-Canada highway" which will link the provinces of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific with a suitable route for motor transport.
It is true, as the report indicates there, that the provincial governments have spent large sums of money on the construction of proper and decent highways. But that result has come about only in the last few years, and I am going to venture this statement: Had it not been for the financial and the industrial improvement in the province of Alberta, that province would never have developed the remarkable system of highways that it now has and which it is continuing: to develop. Because of the provincial government's better standing financially and industrially, we are now beginning to have a greater truck system there, and that is competing materially with railway transportation. That is one of the reasons why today the railway companies and the other vested interests, who are appealing strongly to the government to put transportation under federal control, are greatly concerned because of this competition in trucking. It is remarkable to note in the report that it has been owing largely to the centralization of trucking in central Canada and the competition from the canal rates that Ontario and Quebec have been able to improve their industrial and financial standing to the detriment of the other parts of the country. It is not much wonder, Mr. Chairman, when you read this report over carefully, why the railways and some of the large vested interests of this country have been so bitterly opposed to the free competition of truck transportation. At page 277 of the report they have this to say:
Special mention was made of the desirability of bringing trucks within the same control and regulation as the railways. And here a great obstacle lies in the way. By far the largest part of truck traffic is intra-provincial, and most of this intraprovincial traffic consists of private trucking, that is trucking done by individuals and commercial firms in the handling of their own articles of merchandise. Only a small percentage is trucking for hire. All this intra-provincial truck traffic, both private and for hire, is beyond the jurisdiction of parliament, and this fact presents a barrier to coordination and integration of highway and railway services.
There is one point, Mr. Chairman, where, by reference, the thought is left for the trucking industry to be put under federal control. The minister may not agree with it, but the commission points out very carefully that intra-provincial trucking, that is trucking within the provincial boundaries, comes within the jurisdiction of the provinces without question. But they point out

Supply-Transport
that when it comes to interprovincial trucking there is going to toe difficulty to have co-ordination, and they recommend a one board commission to handle all this transportation.
I said a moment ago that the situation in Ontario and Quebec, because of the trucking competition and the canal competition with the railways, has led to prosperity in those central provinces. Therefore the railways and certain vested interests in this country have used a great deal of pressure to bring the trucking transportation under the board of transport commissioners. If we turn to page 286 of the report we find that Dr. Angus gives some views on it. At the bottom of the page in section 10 he says:
A rate structure, once established, is an important factor in determining the economic location of industry and any change in an established structure is likely in the long run to affect the location of industry by making some enterprises vulnerable to competition.
That is exactly what happened in Ontario and Quebec. Because they had this competition with the rate structure it resulted in a great deal of prosperity for that section of the country. We are not for one moment objecting to prosperity in Ontario and Quebec, tout I am pointing out that that was the fact, and the very fact that the board of transport commissioners and the railways worked together held back the progress of western Canada and the maritimes. And they did it knowingly. Let us not misunderstand that. They did it knowingly, and yet throughout these years the people of the maritimes and the people of the western provinces have appealed in this house and outside to get some fair rate structure established across this country, but to no avail. This report is the first evidence we have ever had of any attempt to be fair in the rates as between eastern and western Canada. The report goes on:
There are, therefore, vested interests-
Notice this. It bears out exactly what I have said in this house for the last two or three years on this question:
There are, therefore, vested interests opposed to any substantial change and insistent that, as a matter of national policy, it should be avoided or neutralized.
They go on:
At the present time a substantial change is taking place in the Canadian rate structure. As in other countries, trucks (whether operating as carriers for hire or owned by shippers) have deprived the railways of much of the revenue which they had previously derived from the carriage of commodities of relatively high value for relatively short distances. The loss in revenue has to be made good from traffic which is not vulnerable to truck competition and, therefore, principally from the carriage of relatively low valued commodities for relatively

long distances. In Canada, more perhaps than elsewhere, the result has been to impose a serious burden on the economies of outlying regions.
There is no doubt in the suggestions of Dr. Angus that the policy which has been laid down by the board of transport commissioners has resulted in rank discrimination against the western provinces particularly as to the advantage of industrial expansion and finances as well. It was rather noticeable to the commissioners that neither Ontario nor Quebec presented a case before the commission. That is understandable. Whether they did so by intent or not, I am not prepared to say, but they were certainly conspicuous by their absence. They already enjoyed the lowest freight rates of anywhere in this country, and only those who are most concerned and who have been deprived of the benefits of those low rates presented their views before the commission.
Let me again draw your attention to page 296 of the report. They put it in a very concise form here, and I think it should be put on the record:
The eloquent silence of Ontario and Quebec in rate cases and in the hearings of this commission points to the effectiveness of truck and water competition in keeping down rates in the St. Lawrence region.
That is very definite. I continue:
More extensive and better highways bring an increase in the density of traffic, greater diversification of industry, lower interest rates on capital . . .
Let me draw to your attention, Mr. Chairman, the fact that that is a very important consideration in the development of industry, which has always been lacking in the western provinces particularly, and I presume in the maritime provinces as well. I continue:
More extensive and better highways bring an increase in the density of traffic, greater diversification of industry, lower interest rates on capital, and even greater extension and improvement of highways. Ability to escape from the full impact of increases in railway rates accentuates the burden of these increases on other regions and compels these regions to concentrate on highway construction as a means of escaping from the burden of higher short haul rates and long haul rates.
That is one of the conditions that have compelled those outlying regions to go in for greater development of hard-surfaced highways. They did not do it for the fun of it. That is a sure thing. Now that we are getting to the point of getting some decent highways-we hope to get a trans-Canada highway soon-the railways and other vested interests are becoming somewhat concerned about who is to control the transportation on those highways. Mind you, these highways are being built by the provinces, and not by any grant of the dominion government, with

the exception of the trans-Canada highway. The commissioners go on in the same paragraph:
Inability to escape the increased burden of higher rates on long haul rail traffic limits the financial strength and restricts the diversification of industry in these regions.
The effectiveness of truck competition in the St. Lawrence region by weakening the financial resources of other regions, limits their possibility of escape from the burden of higher railway rates by means of road construction and motor vehicles.
If the railways can control freight rates through the board of transport commissioners by bringing trucks under the control of the board, then Ontario and Quebec can continue to dominate Canada's field of industry and finance. They will continue to use the maritimes and the prairie provinces as a market for their manufactured goods.
I think that statement is fully borne out by what this report says. So it is not fair and it is not honest and it is not according to facts for anyone to say that there has been no discrimination between east and west. Probably I should make it more definite and say between central Canada, that is Ontario and Quebec, and the western part of Canada. I am more mindful of the western provinces because it is that part from which I come. However, those from the maritime provinces can get up and make their views known. I do not think we would differ much from them because they are in exactly the same industrial and financial position as we are. We have contributed substantially to the advancement of central Canada; it is now time they did a little' contributing toward other parts of Canada.
When I refer to the construction of the trans-Canada highway may I say that I am glad to see it progressing. I have been endeavouring to keep up with the times in the development of that highway, and I can say that the western provinces are developing their share just as quickly as their finances will permit them to do so. I have seen very little development in Ontario in the region between Sault Ste. Marie and Fort William. It is true that there is a good deal of development between Sudbury and Sault Ste. Marie, and from here to those points. In these regions good roads are being constructed; I was over them no later than last fall.
However, it does not make any difference how good the road is to Sault Ste. Marie; if the link between that point and Fort William is missing, what good is it? Anyone who has travelled over the Canadian Pacific Railway has noted, upon looking out of the window, that sections of well-graded gravel road ten to fifteen miles in length have been constructed, but there has been nothing done to

join these sections. This was a terrific waste of money. Do not tell me that was by accident, because I know it was not. That was done years ago to prevent the construction of the trans-Canada highway. Provinces do not build those sections of road at an expense of from $75,000 to $100,000 a mile, and then leave them standing; of course they do not- unless they have very good reasons for doing so.
The provinces concerned are going to have to put up a fight in this field. Some of them are already doing so. I know of only one province that stated before the commission they were prepared to turn the control of trucking over to the federal board, and that was Saskatchewan. I believe they went so far as to say that they would turn over to federal control their internal trucking along the main line. Alberta does not take the same view, nor did any of the other provinces. They can see clearly what has been holding back the progress of those provinces.
Indeed, at page 297 of the report we find this:
The province of Alberta has intimated that it will not give licences for trucks controlled by the railway.
I have come to that part which a while back I indicated to the minister I would read. It is found in the latter part of the second paragraph on page 297, where it says:
Higher interprovincial rates are justified in part by necessity for example in purchasing double licence plates but they present obstacles to trade between provinces and favour intraprovincial trade.

It is of concern to the federal government to institute machinery which will collect full information on the extent of interprovincial trucking.

At -the present time we have been operating under what one of the solicitors for the railways said was not a monopoly but a duopoly. If we put through this other thing we will have a triopoly. I do not know how many more "opolies" we will get as a result. But, as one member suggests, we certainly will have a monopoly. As far as transportation rates are concerned, it will be more than that, we will have a dictatorship.
If you have all these transportation systems under the one board it is safe to say that

while the board will not be made up of the same personnel as the present board it will be quite similar and we will have similar results. Those results -have not been good. They have not been for the benefit of Canada. There should not be a complete monopoly of the transportation systems of this country under any one board.
If the government believes in free enterprise, as it says it does, then we should have free enterprise and free competition.
Would you let the railways set their own rates?

The railways have been setting their own rates, do not make any mistake about that. You have only to refer to the last increases which they asked for and got. The government had something to do with that. That is -the objection to having all these transportation systems under the control of one board. Free competition and free enterprise will have no chance to operate. Therefore I am against the suggestion which I think is made in the report of having transportation by truck under the control of any board or commission.

Mr. Chairman, chapter 5 of the report deals with matters which are of national or local concern, and for a few minutes I should like to deal with a matter of local concern to my constituents. On pages 135 and 136 reference is made to the segregation of passenger and freight revenues and expenses. It was suggested to the commission that any deficit in passenger rates should not be charged to freight rates, but at page 137 of the report the commission recommends:
The freight and passenger services are essential and if the passenger fares cannot be raised to produce sufficient revenue to enable the passenger traffic to pay its own way the freight traffic must bear the burden. The two services are so interrelated that segregation is not practical.
After reading -this conclusion by the commission, we in our section of Ontario are rather perplexed. During the last couple of months the management of Canadian National Railways have been interviewing the heads of municipalities and suggesting that certain passenger services which are now in effect in that section of Ontario should- be discontinued. They propose taking off two passenger trains that run from the divisional -point at Palmerston in my riding to Kincardine and to Southampton. In other words, they propose taking off four trains a day on each of those lines.
It has been proposed to the municipalities that in substitution they will inaugurate three distinct services which will be wholly dependent on gas, rubber and road conditions. They propose to carry express and mail by trucks,

and passengers by busses. I feel that those who are making those recommendations overlook a condition peculiar to our section of the country, that is the road conditions which are created by our weather. As I say, these three services will be dependent upon gas and rubber, which commodities may be in short supply before too long, although we hope that will not be so.
However, the greatest obstacle is the road conditions. I know the type of road condition that is created by the weather in that part of the country because I have lived there all my life. I cannot see how they will be able to keep traffic moving under the conditions which we have at times. I noticed an article in the newspapers yesterday under the dateline Palmerston, April 10, which reads:
Road conditions on local roads have bogged down part of North Wellington district high school buses, and have stalled traffic over a Wellington county-road used as a short cut to Harriston from Palmerston.
That is not an isolated instance because the same condition pertains between Palmerston and Southampton, and even more so between Palmerston and Kincardine. The greatest part of the road that it is proposed to use is a county road. I am quite satisfied that other counties are as much concerned with road costs as is the county of Wellington. At the January session of our county council they decided to set aside one mill for road and bridge improvement, but I notice that in the April session last week they decided that in view of heavy taxation they would forgo that charge and this year they will not be spending that mill. Other counties are finding the burden of keeping up county roads just as heavy as the county in which this proposed service will operate. We are to have four express trucks, four mail trucks and four busses using these county roads.
The railroad company does not propose to stop its freight service. In other words, it will still use these two lines for freight and therefore the roadbeds will have to be kept up. I cannot understand why this additional burden should be passed on to the municipalities when the railroad roadbeds are still to remain. That is something that the people in this part of the province find it hard to understand.
Then there is the employment situation which will result if this proposed change takes place. Palmerston is a divisional point and it has a substantial wartime housing project. Ninety per cent of the houses are occupied by veterans who are employed by Canadian National Railways. If the proposed change goes into effect these men will have to change their place of residence-I
Supply-Transport
do not say they will be out of work because no doubt the railroad can give them employment elsewhere-they will have to move to other divisional points in order to continue working. That means that these men will lose their equity in their houses and the municipality of Palmerston will be faced with the necessity of carrying on where they have left off.
This town has been built around the railroad and as there is no other industry this will mean, quite a serious burden. I do not think anyone will -argue that the railroads in that section of the country have not suffered a loss of considerable passenger traffic. One reason for this is the fact that many people own their own automobiles, but quite a substantial group of people in these communities use a bus line that is operating there. This service is rather uncertain and cannot be considered to be completely dependable by any stretch of the imagination. They run one bus up and one bus down per day on each of the roads I have mentioned.
In his closing remarks the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar referred to the fact that many communities- had been built up on the promise of railroad service. I am thinking of a conversation I had last Saturday with an elderly gentleman in my village. We were not talking about the railway; he just happened to come along and speak to me. He told me that if he lived until May 29 he would be 80 years old, the same age, he said, as the railway track. That just shows how long that service has been in operation.
I think quite a substantial amount of this passenger traffic could be regained by the railways if the management and labour would sit down and talk over the matter. From my own observations in and around Palmerston and other places -affected I believe that if the service were made more attractive, perhaps by using smaller units of some kind, we could continue to carry on almost as in the past. With the weather we have in that part of the country I do not see how trucks and busses can hope to give the kind of service that has been given by the railways; I do not think it can- be done. If I may say so, I believe in the past railways have been rather delinquent in not keeping up with the times. Passing through the villages, towns and cities in our part of the country you will find that one of the most unattractive buildings in- the community will be the local railway station. The bus companies dress up their depots. At the moment I am thinking of the two cities in western Ontario with which I am most familiar, Guelph and Kitchener. The bus depots there

Supply-Transport
are bright buildings with individual chairs, cheerful surroundings and lunch counters. If you go into the Canadian National depots in those cities, however, you find them to be dark, dingy places with hard benches and nothing else. I am sure that if the service were made more attractive more people would use the railways.
Then I believe more advertising should be done. On the afternoon of Easter Sunday I noticed a train running on our line, that is the Southampton line. The track runs right past our farm, and I could see how many people were on the train, I did not know there was going to be a train that afternoon, and I do not think ten people in the village, other than those connected with the railway, knew a train was going to be operated. I was in the village that evening and several people said that if they had known a train would be operating they would have been glad to use it.
So I believe it should be suggested to the Canadian National that they do not take this matter to the board of transport commissioners for approval but that the whole matter be reviewed with the idea of improving the present system. I am quite sure it can be done. I feel that the people of this section of the country, which is one of the most prosperous rural districts in Canada, have a right to expect at least a continuation of the present service, if not an improvement in it, from a government owned and operated transportation system.

I think the hon. member will expect me to comment on the statement he has just made concerning the proposed withdrawal of certain trains on the Palmerston-Kincardine line and perhaps another line which he mentioned. The hon. member has brought up a matter which of necessity concerns the railways from time to time; namely, the unprofitable operation of certain lines. That is evidently what is happening in the area to which the hon. member refers. I am not nearly as familiar with the circumstances as he is, but it may be that the delinquency he charges on the part of the railways arises from the fact that the people are not using the railways. I am reminded of a delegation that came to see me some years ago, not long after I took over responsibility for this department, to protest the withdrawal of certain trains. Upon questioning them it was discovered they had travelled here by bus, not by train. If people in certain areas follow the practice of travelling by bus or in their own cars instead of using the trains, then certainly the people should not be surprised if sooner or later the railway com-

panies make application to the board of transport commissioners for the withdrawal of those trains.
The point here is that the operation is unprofitable because the public are not using the service. The only alternative is for the public to patronize the line. Neither the Canadian National nor any other company can, withdraw a service without the approval of the board of transport commissioners, and in this case I understand the application has not been made as yet. I think the Canadian National Railways have followed the obvious policy of attempting to meet the wishes of the people by discussing with certain public bodies and municipal corporations in the area a method of co-ordinating transportation by operating a portion of the service by rail and a portion by truck. Whether or not it is possible to meet the wishes of the people in the area I am unable to say; but I know those people on behalf of whom the hon. member speaks will have a perfect right to protest the withdrawal of these trains before a public board when the application is made, and give reasons why the service should not be curtailed or withdrawn. I can assure the hon. gentleman that these representations will be given careful consideration by the board.
The hon. member also suggested that the position be reviewed by the Canadian National Railways before the application is launched. I understand that review has been or is being made at the moment, and I am hoping that ways and means may be found to coordinate the services rather than withdraw them entirely.

I do not agree with the
findings of the commission in regard to the Maritime Freight Rates Act. I do not think the maritime provinces get any advantage at all from that act, though the government is paying the railways some $9 million. The special rate on the Canadian National only applies as far as Diamond Junction or Levis. I do not know how far it goes on the Canadian Pacific. Can the minister say the point on the Canadian Pacific to which the 20 per cent applies?
The select territory is set out in the definition section of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, which I can get for the hon. member in a moment.

The select territory is defined in the act. As far as the Canadian National is concerned it is defined as being as far as Diamond Junction. The Canadian Pacific does not go into Diamond Junction. If you are shipping a car of potatoes from New Brunswick to Toronto the increased rates

beyond Diamond Junction take away all the benefits we receive from the Maritime Freight Rates Act. Freight rates have been increased so much that the maritime provinces have been almost put out of business. If east and west cannot ship their goods into central Canada, where the markets have been built up, what are the east and west to do?
The royal commission did not seem to do us much good. They turned down all the requests of the people who appeared before them. They turned down a request that the Maritime Freight Rates Act be extended to include movements to Toronto and Windsor. They turned down the request that the amount be increased to 30 per cent instead of 20 per cent. I do not believe the maritimes have had any advantage from that 20 per cent which was given in about 1926, I think it was, when the act was made effective. I believe that has all been taken away from us now, although the government pays about $9 million into the railways. I believe the railways build up the rates beyond Diamond Junction to cover the 20 per cent by which they have had to reduce the rate before Diamond Junction. I should like the minister to look into that situation, because I think the government is paying out money for nothing.
I should like to find out whether the maritime provinces are getting any advantage out of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. When I went into business we were shipping potatoes to Montreal for 17 cents per hundred. The rate is now 41 cents per hundred, with some other charges added. We have been talking about controls. The bag into which we put 75 pounds of potatoes has gone up 20 cents in the last six months. We used to pay 17 cents. You talk about increasing the cost of living. The increase in the freight rates and the increase in the cost of containers for the potatoes means that a bag of potatoes is costing about 50 cents more than it did a few years ago. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was trying to blame the producer for the increase, but it is not the producer; it is the freight rates. You cannot increase the freight rate and increase the cost of the containers while keeping the price to the consumer at the same level. I should like the minister to look into this situation.
At the time of confederation, when the Intercolonial railway was built, the maritime provinces were promised low freight rates into the markets in central Canada. No attention has been paid to that promise. At the time the Maritime Freight Rates Act was put into effect the rate on potatoes 80709-125

from Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick to Montreal was about 28 cents per hundred. It is now 41 or 42 cents per hundred. I believe the rate is built up beyond Diamond Junction. I do not know where Diamond Junction is, but I believe it is near Levis somewhere. I do not know where the point is on the Canadian Pacific, although they get the advantage of this 20 per cent too. I do not know whether it is St. Johns, Quebec, or Sherbrooke, because the Canadian Pacific does not follow the north shore as does the Canadian National. Perhaps I might be allowed to reply to the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton at this stage. It is true that the main representations by the maritime provinces, with reference to the extension of the select territory and the increase in the subsidy, were not received with approval by the commission. But the representations were carefully studied by the commission, and it is also true that they were made by an important and large group of interests in the maritime provinces. The commission felt that it should not, for the reasons given in the report, extend the select territory, nor should it increase the 20 per cent to 30 per cent.
But the commission did accept one of the main requests of the maritime provinces, and that was in regard to the complaint that horizontal rate increases were burdensome on them, and had a detrimental effect upon the Maritime Freight Rates Act itself. After investigation of that complaint, the commission felt that there was a great deal to be said for it, and recommended to the board that hereafter it should not grant horizontal increases across the board, but that the increases should be granted in the manner in which they were granted originally by the board after it was established back in 1903.
What was the original plan, to increase in districts and areas?

That was one plan, and there was another plan which was given in detail in the report. Prior to 1914, I believe, the plan was one which increased the rates in western Canada less than in central Canada. I think there was, as well, a basis for a percentage increase in the eastern provinces.

The railways have not followed the terms of the act. They have not kept separate accounts up to Diamond Junction or any other place. They are supposed to keep those accounts.
