I hope that such a subsidy will be paid by the government. I trust that it will do a great deal of good in removing discrimination. But I want to point out that $7 million in the budget of the Canadian National Railways or of the Canadian Pacific Railway-and it would have to be apportioned between the two of them-is not a large percentage of the income of either system. It is probably something less than one per cent of the total income of the two railway systems. If all we get out of this report, or if all the action the government will take is the payment of that $7 million, I doubt that that will have any great impact on the matter of discrimination.
I know that this problem of attempting to equalize freight rates across Canada is a difficult one. I am sure it is difficult; otherwise the board of transport commissioners, in making their awards, would have made the freight rates equal. Whenever you get a

Supply-Transport
difference in freight rates because of competitive rates in central Canada and higher rates on the prairies and elsewhere, and then get the railways in a position where they need an increase in revenue, in a situation like that it is extremely difficult to bring the competitive rates up sufficiently to provide for that increase and hence to assist in equalization. Even with all of the good recommendations of the royal commission, I do not think freight rates in themselves can be equalized without exception throughout Canada unless something more is done. Instead of a $7 million subsidy only, I say that the federal government should be prepared to subsidize the financial needs of the Canadian railways-both the C.N.R. and the C.P.R.- to whatever extent is necessary in order to provide equal freight rates throughout all parts of Canada. We on the prairies suffer because of a national policy which meant higher freight rates and tariff walls. I think the time has now arrived when the government should implement a policy which will, in fact, once and for all permanently remove discrimination and that the government should take into consideration the proposal set forth in the submission of the Saskatchewan government to the royal commission, namely, after all other steps have been taken to remove discrimination, to consider whatever subsidy is necessary in order that discrimination may be finally removed.
I notice that while the report does not recommend that the board of transport -commissioners acquire the jurisdiction of handling truck traffic in interprovincial trade, nevertheless the royal commission suggests that parliament should consider dealing with the matter of truck competition in interprovincial trade. If the government would equalize freight rates throughout Canada, then I for one am all for the board of transport commissioners or some other government body having control over trucks in interprovincial trade. But until that time comes I shall view with misgiving any acquiring, by the board of transport commissioners or by any other government body, of control over truck rates in interprovincial trade. On the prairies we have no water competition. The truck competition that we have is relatively small, but nevertheless it is a growing competition. I am afraid that in some respects the railway companies are pricing themselves out of the market. Freight rates on automobiles from Oshawa and Windsor to Regina are apparently so high now that fleets of trucks can bring new automobiles into Saskatchewan at a considerable saving. I have here a bulletin put out by the Saskatchewan Motor Dealers' Association; and it refers to one truck dealer in Saskatchewan who saved $4,400 out of a

total freight bill of $7,000, by bringing his trucks in saddle-mounted or by a piggy-back type of transportation.
If, in addition to the discrimination which already exists, the government should take control of the trucking industry in interprovincial traffic without first having removed discrimination, then that can only result in further -discrimination against the prairies, British Columbia, the maritimes and those areas of Canada outside of the central provinces. Before any move is made to control the trucking industry I say that the first and the most important move is to undertake effective steps to remove -discrimination and to bring about implementation of the suggestion in this report that equalization in freight rates should be accomplished. I hope the government will -bring in during this session whatever amendments it thinks are necessary. I hope it will take whatever action is necessary to see that the board of transport commissioners conclude their general inquiry into freight rates and -deal with this matter of discrimination -and equalization which, in the fina-l analysis, even under this report, is left to the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners.

Just before the dinner recess I asked the minister a question in regard to -select territory on the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian National railway. I understand that the Canadian Pacific railway -point is Boundary. Boundary is east of Megantic. That is not a comparable point with Diamond Junction. That is about 125 miles short of the point called Diamond Junction.
In New Brunswick a person shipping over the Canadian Pacific railway has less advantage than a person in New Brunswick shipping over the Canadian National railway. This point of Boundary should- be changed to Farnham, Quebec. I see that the only recommendation the commission make is that section 6 of the act should be changed in regard to keeping a separate account so that they will conform to the present practice of breaking the law. I have never heard of a recommendation like that before. At present it seems that the railways pay no attention to section 6 of the act. I cannot find out how the accounts of the Maritime Freight Rates Act are kept. The government knows where the rates are in effect. It looks to me as though the shipper in Nova Scotia gets more advantage than the shipper in New Brunswick. The shipper in Newfoundland would get still more advantage.
In regard to export trade the act refers to shipments between Fredericton and Saint

John, and from Fredericton to Liverpool. The act defines freight between Fredericton and Saint John, New Brunswick. All the export freight originates north of Fredericton, New Brunswick, or practically all of it. There is practically no advantage whatever in this part of the act. I do not suppose that half a dozen carloads of freight originates in Fredericton, or between Fredericton and Saint John for export; therefore the shippers north of Fredericton have no advantage, and that is where practically 90 per cent of the export freight in New Brunswick originates.
I should like the minister to look into this. The act should be amended regardless of the recommendation of the commission. They do not do anything but recommend that the act be repealed so that the railways can conform with what they have done. They have broken the law all along since September 26, 1926, and the commission wants them to continue to break the law. That is all they recommend in the report. It is something like the flour milling report.
Now, with regard to trucking competition-
Combination.

You are forcing trucking competition. The increase in freight rates is forcing every person into the trucking business. I agree there should be some dominion regulation with regard to trucking, but so long as you go on increasing your freight rates to the east and west, something has to be done. Ontario and Quebec have the advantages of the trucks and of the railways. They have all the advantages. Something has to be done in the east and the west so that they will have a decent rate into the central markets. So long as you maintain the markets in the two provinces of central Canada and you keep building up those provinces under the defence act, and in every other way, something will have to be done between the railways in eastern Canada and the railways in western Canada, and also something will have to be done about the trucks. I know the railways are going to put themselves out of business if they keep on increasing their rates.
There is a very bad trucking arrangement now between the provinces. There should be some uniformity in the regulations between provinces. You can carry so much on a truck in one province and so much in another province. When you get to the border of another province you have to change. In other words, in the province of Quebec you cannot operate a truck on Sunday. If a trucker picks up a load in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick and gets to the Quebec border on Saturday, he has to
Supply-Transport
lay up over Sunday. The railways do not stop for Sunday. They are allowed to operate on Sunday. They go right on. The trucker has to stop and has to wait there until Monday morning before he can start off with his truck again. He has to wait until after twelve o'clock on Sunday night.
This week I had occasion to send a truck to Montreal for a piece of machinery. The piece of machinery could not be carried by freight; it had to be carried very carefully on a truck. We did not think it was advisable to put it in a railway car. That piece of machinery had to be hauled in pieces to the United States border on a small truck, on account of the regulations in the province of Quebec. Then it could be taken with a large truck from the border a distance of some five hundred or six hundred miles to its destination in New Brunswick. There are all kinds of different regulations. They have the same trouble in the United States. You can take a certain load over some state roads, and when you get to the border of another state you have to leave part of your load and come back and get it. There should be some regulation with regard to trucks, a federal regulation. So long as you keep increasing the freight rates you are bound to have trucking, and you are bound to have truck competition, especially east and west.
I should like the minister to take all these things into consideration. With regard to the Maritime Freight Rates Act, as it is now, after you get up to Diamond Junction boundary the rate is built up to take all the advantage of the 20 per cent that the maritime provinces get. Diamond Junction boundary on the Canadian Pacific Railway should be changed to Sherbrooke or Magog or Farnham, a comparable point with the Canadian National railway point. The Canadian Pacific railway shipper from New Brunswick should not be discriminated against.

I should like to join with
others for a minute in welcoming this report. The west has been waiting for a report of this kind for many, many years. If its object of removing some of the grievances that the west has carried for these many- years is fulfilled it will have accomplished what it set out to do.
I should like briefly to refer to two items. One is the recommendation of a federal subsidy to cover a portion of the costs between the east and west from Fort William to Sudbury. I think a tribute is due to the present leader of the opposition in the province of Saskatchewan. So far as my knowledge goes, he is one of the first men in Canada

Supply-Transport
to bring to our attention the need of a subsidy to equalize the rates between the east and west in that area.
Then, the other point to which I should like to refer is a reference to a railway in my constituency of Maple Creek. That reference appears at page 133 of the report, where the Fill-the-Gap association presented its report to the commission regarding the necessity that has existed in that area ever since the country was first settled. The pioneers in that country came there about forty years ago, one of the incentives being that they were promised a railway at that time. At the present time there is a railway, but there is a round-trip backhaul of about 200 miles. These people must suffer because of increased freight rates on their grain, increased rates on their livestock as well as other rates. Then they have to suffer the depreciation in the value of the livestock that has travelled that extra distance over a railway, slow as railways can be - on some of the branch lines in western Canada.
It is not overestimating at all to say that hundreds of thousands of dollars have been lost by farmers in those areas because of the increased freight rates, and in my opinion the railway itself has lost large sums of money by this backhaul which could be eliminated by the completion of only thirty-five miles of line up the two branch lines and make it possible to ship livestock and grain direct.
As everyone knows, these people are twenty-five miles from the nearest railway. One can imagine the difficulties they encounter, particularly in wintertime, when they are locked in for months at a time without any access to those services which we in our modern civilization would ordinarily demand. They are long distances from doctors and the other amenities of life. These people have been in that position for so long that they have now adopted the attitude that unless something is done soon it will never be done. This subject has been discussed for so many years that they have abandoned hope of ever having that which was promised them at the beginning.
When one waits all one's life for a train it is as bad as waiting all one's life for those other things for which one has wished since boyhood. I believe the time has come when the people of that area might rightfully demand from the powers who control these railways either that the railway be completed, or that some alternative method be devised to alleviate the desperate situation there. Otherwise they will have to abandon hope absolutely. Therefore I would ask that the government, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the board of transport commissioners use

their influence to contribute to some extent to the permanency of the district so as to fulfil, before it is too late, the expectations of the pioneers of that country.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two on the matter of transportation, and the various activities which come under the direction of the Minister of Transport. I shall say nothing whatever about the report of the royal commission on transportation. There have been a good many speeches on that already, and they have covered the field very well. I should like to support the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre.
At this time too I would extend my congratulations to the newly appointed parliamentary assistant to the minister. I had four points in mind with which I should like to deal. Perhaps I should have waited until they were called, but I thought if I dealt with them now we would save time later.
The first of these, one with which I have dealt before, is the discriminatory rate on soybeans from the western Ontario area to Toronto. The soybean growers pay the same rate as is paid on flaxseed. Yet it is just as easy to transport soybeans as to transport wheat or coarse grains. On the other hand I realize that the transportation of flaxseed is a different and more difficult matter. Therefore I would ask the parliamentary assistant to look into that matter.
Then, there is another sore point across the country, and particularly in my area, in connection with the collection of radio licence fees. Since putting a question on the order paper some time ago I have had a number of letters in protest against some of the things that have happened. In one instance a certain man had come to a neighbourhood and sold licence fees through the years. Last year however, either because the man had died or had got a better job, or for some other reason, he did not make the customary call. In consequence the radio inspector who was making a check penalized this man and a good many of his neighbours who, because they had been waiting for the annual call of the man in question, had failed to get their licences. The man had promised that he would come each year. They failed to obtain their licences, not because they were trying to evade the law but because they were trying to do business through their friend. Many people think that a radio licence is more a nuisance than anything else, and I believe much credit would come to the government if it were to abolish the licence altogether, and have done with it.

The next item with which I shall deal has reference to the fund set up for the elimination of dangerous crossings. I doubt whether the crossing to which I shall now refer is in need of a subway or overpass. However it is on highway No. 22 just east of Calamity Corners at London. Some years ago there was a serious accident at that point, upon which occasion the hon. member for Middlesex West approached the department. The superintendent 'of the Stratford division inspected the crossing and said, "Well, it is clear. There is good vision from all directions, and it would cost $4,000 to instal warning signals". Strange as it may seem several accidents have happened there. There is bush both east and west to the north of the highway, and apparently it is not as easy to see a train at that point as one would imagine.
The result was that on March 31 of this year four American tourists were killed at that crossing. I should think that $4,000 would be a small price to pay when one considers that already four lives have been lost, and that there have been other accidents as well. Now, with the building of the new high school at Arva, twice a day the school busses will have to cross that dangerous crossing. I am hoping, along with the hon. member for Middlesex West, who brought the matter to the minister's attention after another serious accident, that further investigation will be made, and that crossing signals will be installed.
Then there is the question to which I referred about three sessions ago, namely the improvement of the runways at London airport. I said at that time that apparently North Star aircraft could go anywhere in the world but to London. In these days, with the jet fighter aircraft longer runways will be required. I would hope therefore that the minister would take care of this matter, for the benefit of the London area.

May I comment on the railway grade crossing accident to which the hon. member referred? Not only has this matter been brought to my attention at this time, it was raised also by the hon. member for Middlesex West. It was a serious accident and the board of transport commissioners are conducting an investigation. The question of protection is one for the authorities owning or controlling the highway. If it is a municipal or county road, then the municipality or the county council would have to make application to the board to have some sort of wigwag or signal protection. I am sure that if the municipalities concerned were to do that, in view of the seriousness of the accident the board would give it careful
Supply-Transport
consideration. My experience has been that where the cost is not too high the board as a rule grants the application.
This is number 22 provincial highway.
Then the application would be made by the province.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take up much of the time of the committee but I must express my disapproval of one thing that is taking place in my section of the country. This is an old settled farming district populated by people of English, Irish and Scotch descent, although there are also other nationalities. I consider this district to be second to none.
We are informed that our passenger train service is to be cut off completely for a distance of 82 railroad miles, which would be about 100 highway miles.
Where is this?

Between Palmerston and Kincardine. Kincardine is on the shores of lake Huron and at the end of the line, while Palmerston is the divisional point where you change to go to different parts of western Ontario. Tenders have been called for to provide a mail service by truck. I am informed that from 157 to 200 bags of mail are sent up this line daily which will give some idea of the number of people being served.
We are located in a snow belt and there have been times in my day and age when even the railroad was tied up with snow for as long as three weeks. It will be realized how difficult it will be to transport mail oy truck. I am informed that these trucks will have to move on schedule and be at a certain place at a certain time. If the elements say you are not moving, you just stay in a snowbank and you may be there for days.
Many people will be thrown out of work, not only those employed on the railroad but those who carry mail from the station to the post office. The trucks will now deliver direct to the post office. This change will be rather severe on some of these men. Not long ago the government took over the Temiscouata railroad and I should like to ask the minister what was the operating loss on that road and what population is served by it?
There are at least 100,000 people being served by this line. I do not intend to discuss freight rates but I should like to tell a true story. You sometimes hear of people shooting the bull but last week I bought a bull and shipped him from Montreal to my home

Supply-Transport
town of Brussels. You should have seen the expressions on the faces of the expressmen when they had to lift the bull out of the express car. It will be seen what kind of mess our freight rates are in when I state that I was able to ship that bull cheaper by express than by freight.
This matter of cutting off the passenger train service is not a political issue because the hon. member for Wellington North spoke about this matter this afternoon. I was not in the chamber when he spoke but he must be affected and felt that there was something wrong because he is on the government side of the house. We do not want this service discontinued.
I understand that it is still intended to run one freight train a day, but they intend to take off the two passenger trains per day which are now operating. It will mean that these people will have no passenger train service at all and only one freight train a day. Express and mail will be handled by truck. If this matter was important to the hon. member for Wellington North, it is doubly important to me and even more important to people living farther up the line. We are about 40 miles from the end of the line.
As I say, we are in a snow belt. While the facilities for the removing of snow are much better today than they used to be, the fact remains that when you have a storm lasting nine days, which happens quite often, you just cannot move at all. I would ask the minister to take this change into serious consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the hon. gentleman that the discontinuance of a train or any service is of importance. This matter is so important that parliament decided in 1903 that services could not be discontinued or a service curtailed without a hearing before the board of transport commissioners. When the hon. member for Wellington North brought this matter to my attention this afternoon I indicated to him at some length just what procedure would have to be followed by the railway before it could stop the service.
The hon. member who has just spoken seems to be of the opinion that this matter is settled and decided, but such is not the case. An application will have to be made by the Canadian National Railways to discontinue the train service, and) the municipalities affected^ or individuals if they so desire, can protest and the board, which is a court of record, will determine the issue. I am sure that the speeches made by the hon. member for Wellington North and the hon. gentleman 
who has just taken his seat will be brought to the attention of the board of transport commissioners.
The hon, member asked some questions about the purchase of the Temiscouata railway by the government. The circumstances there are entirely different. The Temiscouata railway was a continuation of a line which the Canadian National Railways could take over. The population in that area is about 35,000 or 40,000. There were no operating results of the Temiscouata railway available, as I indicated to the house when the bill was brought down. If the hon. gentleman would take the trouble to look at that debate, which is now two years old, I think he will find all the information he wants.
What profits have been made since the C.N.R. took it over?

If my hon. friend will ask that question next week when the railways and shipping committee is sitting and the president of the Canadian National Railways is here, I believe that would be the best way to pursue the matter. I think the answer will be that there are no separate accounts kept of the four various regions-prairies, Pacific, maritimes and central-that make up the national system.

I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that whether or not a decision has been reached they have already asked for tenders for the carriage of mail by truck. They have gone a long way if they do not intend to take off the trains.

I cannot be responsible for anyone asking for tenders. I can be responsible only for the matters under my jurisdiction, and I am telling my hon. friend that the Canadian National Railways must have the authority of the board of transport commissioners before curtailing the service. That is the practice.

I want to say just one tiny word in respect to the report of the royal commission on transportation, and that word will be confined to one subject in which I am particularly interested. I have not read the report with meticulous care, but I have glanced through it quite thoroughly in an attempt to find whether or not the subject of coal subventions to railways was dealt with; and I have looked in vain. The only reference I can find to the matter is on page 85, where we are given information which of course we already know. I shall take a moment to read it:
Rates on coal were introduced in 1925 by arrangement with the federal government and reduced to $8 a ton in 1934 as an emergency measure to relieve unemployment in Alberta. At present the rate is

$8.40 of which the shipper pays $5.90 and the government $2.50. The normal rate from Drum-heller to Toronto is $13.10.
That was all the consolation I found as I browsed through this report in an endeavour to find out what might be expected in future in respect to subventions on coal. I know, of course, that the actual payment of coal subventions comes under the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys; nevertheless subventions are paid the railway companies for the movement of coal, and I had rather expected that something would be said about it in the report. I am particularly interested because of the present threat of higher freight rates, and the further threat of the removal of subventions. If this should be done I am afraid the coal mining industry of western Canada will fold up, that its days will be numbered. I am glad to see the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys in his seat. He is one of the Alberta representatives, and I trust that he will view his responsibilities with such seriousness that he will attempt to keep the coal mining industry of Canada on its feet. It will not be kept on its feet if there is an increase in the freight structure affecting coal, or if coal subventions are removed. I say this to him now, and perhaps will have a little more to say when his estimates come before the house.
There is another matter I should like to take up with the minister, departing now from the report of the transportation commission. At times the coal mining industry of western Canada is seriously affected by a shortage of cars. I am sure the minister is aware of that situation, and perhaps it is not an easy matter to deal with. This is a serious thing because when there is a shortage of cars the coal mines close down and several thousand coal miners are out of work for perhaps several days until cars arrive on the scene. That is not a good thing, but it has happened many times over the last few years, to the detriment of the coal mining industry itself. In the first place the coal miners are laid off three or four days a week, although of course not every week. The other point is that even though they are not operating and actually mining coal, the mines have to stay open. The power plants have to be kept running; many of the staff, engineers and so forth, have to be at their posts, and this is an added burden upon the coal mining companies. This all results from the shortage of cars. I wish the minister would reply on this point, because it is serious and I do not want to have to wire or telephone or write to him when that happens. I would have to do it every week or two, and anyway it is not my business to do that. I emphasize the
Supply-Transport
seriousness of the situation and beg the minister to do something to remedy it.
My particular interest in my constituency, of course, lies in the Crowsnest pass. The Canadian Pacific Railway runs through that pass; nevertheless the Minister of Transport, if his title means anything, must use his influence in respect to all transportation problems. There is one other small matter I want to bring up, though it does not affect my constituency and perhaps I should not mention it. Lately it has been my privilege to take a trip or two over the Canadian National between Edmonton and Ottawa. I am amazed at what I would term the deterioration of the roadbed of the Canadian National Railways in that territory. I know that you have to spend1 a lot of money when you begin reinforcing and repairing roadbeds. I do not know whether the minister has been over that road. I usually travel on the other railway because it is more convenient.
I go over it every year.

I am pleased to note that the minister is alive to tell the tale. My only consolation as I was going over that railroad recently was that I had taken out three days' insurance at twenty-five cents a day. It was rather slim consolation, because they would only pay my estate $5,000. I thought the train was going to jump those tracks at any moment. The minister has been over the road, and he knows it. He must have eaten a meal on the railroad, I do not know whether the minister drinks-he must drink something. I shall challenge the minister to sit in the club car of that train anywhere between Edmonton and Ottawa, pick up a glass of gingerale and drink it without spilling it on his vest. If he can do that, he is a better conjurer than I am. When he eats his meals he must be careful or he will find he is feeding his ear instead of his mouth. I do not know if that situation can be remedied. I do not suppose a railway is going to spend several million dollars just to help the passengers drink gingerale, but the roadbeds are deteriorating and I believe something should be done.

May I be allowed to reply to the two points raised by the member for Macleod. I am sorry that I must tell him I have not been advised of any shortage of coal cars in western Canada. Over the last few weeks, months as a matter of fact, I have been advised of a shortage of box cars for the movement of grain. I am prepared to deal with that, but since it has not been raised there is no point in discussing it. I shall ask my officers if they are aware of any threatened shut-down of the mines

Supply-Transport
because of a shortage of cars. My experience over the years has been that we have always had a substantial number of coal cars in Canada, but that at certain times of the year we were short of box cars. Fortunately, at the present time, I believe the box car situation has remedied itself. 1 shall be glad to bring to the attention of the Canadian National Railways the condition to which the member for Macleod refers.
As I said a moment ago, I go to the western part of Canada and out to the coast once a year. I cannot recollect any experience such as that outlined by the member. However, I am sure he would not bring it up unless he was quite satisfied that the facts were as he alleges. I shall be glad1 to bring it to the attention of the officers of the railway.

The minister indicated in the course of his remarks that he had not been asked to comment on the subject of grain cars. I would be only too glad to ask him at this moment to do so. Back in the part of Canada whence I come, the situation has been extremely critical. In my own town, for example, there are approximately seven elevators. Two months ago they were packed to the roof with 700,000 bushels of wheat, much of which was damp and tough. It was estimated that in that area there were approximately 500,000 bushels of grain still on the farms, much of it damp and tough.
I am fully aware of the problem with which the board is confronted in connection with not only drying that type of grain, but the sale of it. With the approach of warm weather, the situation is going to become even more critical. On top of that, of course, is the fact that many of these farmers, having been unable to sell their grain, are experiencing certain financial difficulties. I understand that the wheat board did consult with the railroads, urging that there be a better allocation of grain cars for the movement of this grain. This is what I observed in my constituency. Where we had two lines of railroad, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, paralleling each other, both companies were moving in quite a number of grain cars. But on the line between Red Deer and Calgary for example, where we had no comparable competition, the Canadian Pacific appeared just a bit remiss in what I might call its duty in moving in these grain cars. I fully appreciate the problem, but I would ask the minister if there has been any appreciable change within the last month, and if not what these farmers might be able to expect in the way of relief from the current problem.

As I indicated before, the
situation, while it was rather serious some weeks ago, has bettered itself substantially, as I shall indicate in a moment. I believe the causes were, first, the switchmen's strike in the United States, and then the blizzard in western Canada which tied up a number of box cars in certain areas. Then again, there is always a heavy movement of paper and other export products from Canada to the United States. This shortage has led to protests from various bodies in western Canada as well as other parts of Canada.
The picture on April 9, as it has been handed to me, is as follows. I should like to put on Hansard the unfavourable position of box cars generally from February 16 to date, because it was at that time the position was the worst. On February 16, Canadian box cars on United States lines numbered 29,989; United States box cars on Canadian lines amounted to 13,544. Therefore, the unfavourable balance to Canadian lines was 16,445. A month later, on March 16, Canadian box cars on United States lines had reached the total of .31,682; United States box cars on Canadian lines numbered 15,530. The unfavourable balance to Canadian lines was 16,152. On March 30, Canadian box cars on United States lines numbered 31,725; United States box cars on Canadian lines amounted to 17,300. The unfavourable balance was 14,425. On April 8, 29,132 Canadian box cars on United States lines; 18,327 United States box cars on Canadian lines. The unfavourable balance was 10,805.
It will be noted from the above statement that there has been a reduction between the earliest date, February 16, and April 8 of some 800 box cars on United States lines. On the other hand there has been a substantial increase of United States box cars on Canadian lines, to the amount of 4,800, making a net improvement in the unfavourable position of Canadian box cars of 5,640 cars. On March 9, which was the peak in the interchange position, the unfavourable balance stood at 18,935. Therefore since that time an improvement of over 10,000 cars has taken place. A moment ago I said that the unfavourable balance as of April 8 was 10,805. The normal position is about 8,000 in Canada. We have therefore almost reached the normal position. That is indicated by a letter which I have in my possession from the chief commissioner of the Canadian wheat board dated April 9. I quote from it. It states:
I am pleased to advise that the improvement in Vancouver loadings is continuing and although we are on demurrage on some of our boats in Vancouver, if the railways will continue to step up their

loadings and will move the wheat quickly to Vancouver, we can cut down on prospective demurrage claims.
I am glad to advise also that the over-all car loadings are better. On Friday we had close to 1,000 cars loaded with grain in the whole of the western division, and on Saturday, 870 cars, the break-down by provinces being Manitoba, 121; Saskatchewan, 409; Alberta, 340; and the break-down between railways, C.P.R., 430; C.N.R., 428; N.A.R., 12.
Then he adds:
The following boats are either at Fort William or due at Fort William:
Now at Fort William:	Hochelaga, Coverdale,
Ashcroft, Lemoyne, Stadacona, Hagarty.
Due Tuesday:	Prescott.
Due Wednesday:	Westmount.
We expect these boats will load within a day or two, just as soon as they can get into elevators. This early opening is quite encouraging.
I think the position has bettered itself because of the two things which were done by the department officials and which I mentioned before, but more particularly because of the committees which were established among the railways, the shipping companies, the Department of Transport officials and others who were interested in the movement of grain. Those people had preliminary meetings; and because of the action which they took they were, I think, instrumental in bringing about a position which is almost back to normal, I am happy to say.

There has been a great deal
of discussion this afternoon and evening with respect to the report of the royal commission on the freight rates structure. Much of that discussion has come from western members, and it might be expected that those of us from the east would also deal with this problem at some length. Certainly we have both suffered from the same disability with respect to the incidence of freight rates. The fact that possibly those of us in the east may not be quite as vocal as some of the western members in expressing their grievances with respect to this matter would not for one moment suggest that the load is any more easy to bear.
As I think the minister knows, we have in the maritime provinces, representing the various provincial governments and boards of trade, a freight rate commission which has given this matter considerable attention. I am advised by some officers of that commission that they are meeting now and over the week end and are giving further study to the report of this royal commission. Of course their findings or recommendations are not necessarily those which members of this committee generally or any one of them in particular would accept. But we all realize 80709-126
S upply-Transport
that this is a complicated and involved subject; and certainly, so far as I am concerned, I would prefer to have their analysis of the situation, and their criticisms and suggestions with respect to the report, before attempting to deal adequately with this matter before the house. I simply make that as an explanation for the reason why I at any rate am not attempting to deal with the report of this commission tonight. But I presume that at some time in the near future the minister's estimates will again be before us, and probably on the matter of the Maritime Freight Rates Act or some other item such as that we will then have the opportunity to discuss the report of the commission, having regard to its incidence in the maritime provinces. Certainly we have a tremendous interest in this problem. It is an old one as far as the east is concerned. The matter of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, to which the royal commission referred, has been of tremendous help to the maritimes in the past but that help has decreased, unfortunately, or diminished owing to the lessening of freight rates in Ontario and Quebec because of the competition of motor trucks and the other factors with which we are all familiar.
The hon. member for Cumberland was a member of the government of the province of Nova Scotia which first started the agitation for the old Duncan commission or the maritime rights commission. Out of that maritime rights commission came the Duncan report; and as a result of that report we obtained the Maritime Freight Rates Act. Certainly all of us in the east appreciate the work which was done by that commission and the leadership which was given to it by the hon. member for Cumberland and others. As I said, the effect or the benefit of the act is far less today than we should like to have it. Personally, I think the whole matter will have to be reviewed in the near future. Consideration should be given to amendments to the act. But as I said, I would not attempt to discuss this matter in detail now because I think we should first of all receive the benefit of all the advice we can get on that subject.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer briefly. It is one that is not covered by the royal commission at all but it is one coming under the aegis of the minister, although unfortunately there is no specific item in his department for it. Generally, it would come under marine services. It is the unfortunate fact that we at least in the east have not at this time-

Supply-Transport
and I do not believe those on the west coast have either-a coastguard service to be of assistance to those on the sea.
We had in the east last year a most unfortunate tragedy, and there have been many of them. The one of which I am thinking at the moment occurred last fall, when fishing boats were at sea. A tornado swept up the coast. The weather report had been given at midnight saying the weather was fine; and the men in the little boats largely went to sleep feeling that everything was all right. An hour later hurricane warnings were suddenly issued; but there was no one to tell the crews of those boats that the weather had changed so quickly and so dramatically. In the early hours of the morning the storm swept up and some of those boats were drifting for days. At least one of them was lost, with the loss of five of the crew. For three days one could hear the wireless telephone trying to communicate with someone, trying to get a rescue ship directed to their attention. Appeals were made to private ships. They went out. They in turn appealed to the United States coastguard service; and we owe a tremendous debt to the work of the United States coastguard. That service has always responded whenever we have called upon it for assistance. In this case they answered the call. One cutter was 91 miles away. This was after the boats had been drifting for twenty-four hours. They said, "We will be there in six hours". They came but still they could not find the boat. They called in another United States cutter, and we had two American coastguard cutters patrolling there for two or three days. Finally after a week one of these boats, which was lost, was found, with the bodies of three of the crew afloat in the cabin, partially submerged; they had been alive no one knows how long. But the boat had capsized and they were adrift and floating in the water in the cabin. If an adequate service had been available, that tragedy could have been averted. That is only one of many tragedies of the kind which occur along the coast line of the Atlantic and also, undoubtedly, on the Pacific. The only hope of averting them is to call for the assistance of the United States coastguard. I know that the search and rescue squadron of the R.C.A.F. has done a tremendous amount in connection with searching for missing boats, and we owe to the men of the R.C.A.F. a great debt for the work they have done. But aeroplanes, even Cansos and amphibians, cannot land in rough seas. They cannot find ships in a fog nor can they find small boats such as fishing craft and similar ones.

We have off the Nova Scotia coast today a tremendous tourist industry. We have the swordfishing industry, which is advertised all over the world, bringing tourists there in small boats by the score, going out in rough waters and trusting in time of trouble to the United States coastguard to come to their assistance. The minister might tell us that instructions have been given for co-ordination between the R.C.A.F. and other ships under his control, ships of the department of marine and probably cutters of the R.C.M.P. as well. If there have been instructions for such co-ordination, Mr. Chairman, it does not work, because there were no boats under the Canadian flag available for the episode off Woods Harbour for days after the tragedy occurred. I believe it was four days after the ship was first reported missing before the R.C.M.P. cutter got there, and the Americans had searched during that period of time.
I am not criticizing the men of the R.C.M.P. or others. We just have not got the ships available. It is no good to have co-ordination with a ship on the Northumberland strait if you need it for the Yarmouth light or vice versa. I suggest it is a reflection upon Canada that we are depending upon our United States friends in times such as these. I do think economically it is bad because the loss of life and the loss of property, and the threat of this loss hanging over the heads of the industry, fishing, tourist and otherwise, is an economic liability which could be and should be obviated in the future. I realize the necessity for economy and all the rest of it, but we also realize, sir, that even in times such as these it is necessary not to have too much economy if this country is to prosper as a united nation. We in the east, and probably the same thing is true in the west,' think that this is a service which is deficient today. It is a service which we need. I am asking the minister and urging him and this government to give attention to it and that within the reasonably near future a coastguard service be created, which will be of real assistance to us and will help to maintain the traditions of the sea of which we are so proud in Canada.

The matter of a coastguard service for Canada was debated and discussed in this house at some length on at least two different occasions each year. The result of the discussions was that an interdepartmental committee, consisting of a number of representatives of government departments, was established to consider co-ordination of marine search and rescue services. The committee arrived at certain very definite conclusions, which were outlined later by

the Minister of National Defence in the house, since the responsibility was his, and is his hereafter. But since at the time it concerned the department over which I presided I feel that I should make some reply to the statements which my hon. friend has made, and which are not at all accurate.
The decision which was taken by the committee was that the R.C.A.F. be designated as the co-ordinating agency through its centres at Halifax, Trenton and Vancouver, and other government departments concerned were to co-operate fully with the R.C.A.F. That meant that the R.C.A.F. were given the task of co-ordinating the various government ships such as R.C.M.P. patrol boats, Department of Transport ships and Department of National Defence ships, in conjunction too with the air services branch of national defence. The R.C.A.F. is to set up a system of communication, with the other departments co-operating, so that casualties may be reported promptly. Necessary publicity is given to this search and rescue organization so that the public and interested agencies will know the appropriate action to take in the event of a casualty. Copies of this directive have been issued to each of the district marine agencies of the Department of Transport and to all other departmental ships concerned.
I have here a detailed list of those instructions. When the decision was taken and approved of, the Minister of National Defence made a statement in the house outlining the position. At that time he indicated a number of cases where government services had gone to the assistance of United States casualties, United States ships found in distress, and they were far more numerous, if my memory serves me correctly, than the cases where the United States coastguard cutters had come to the assistance of Canadians. I do not mean by that that there is no cooperation between the two. There is. But in case the committee should have the mistaken opinion that it is only the United States coastguard cutters that come to the assistance of our people, may I say that such is not the case.
Another feature of this is that in the Department of Transport at least clear and definite instructions have been given to our ships-and I am sure that obtains in other departments-that the moment they are advised by the R.C.A.F. of a casualty they are to leave their duties and go to the assistance of the ship in distress. I am not familiar with the case to which my hon. friend refers, but I can tell him this, that the committee that dealt with it gave it very 80709-1261

careful consideration. They spent many months dealing with the problem. They heard evidence from persons interested on the west coast and from other interested departments, and came to the conclusion that the best method which could be adopted was that of co-ordination under the direction of the R.C.A.F.

It was not my intention to take part at any great length in the debate that has been in progress for quite a little while. But since it has been centred around the report of the royal commission on transportation, perhaps the committee might think that Prince Edward Island was a hundred per cent in favour of the report if I did not say something. I should like to draw attention to a few things with which I myself cannot agree.
Royal commissions are always very valuable in obtaining a great deal of information, and they are fact finding; but the unfortunate part of it is that when they present their reports to the government the government still has the right to ignore their findings and not to carry them into effect. I know that is true of a royal commission we had in 1926 which was known as the Andrew Rae Duncan commission. It brought in some excellent recommendations to the government, and I must say that it was a long time before we could get any government to implement those recommendations.
To my province of Prince Edward Island transportation is a vital thing. The union of Canada was formed on transportation. The upper provinces did not have any seaports. Their trade was growing. They looked around and inveigled New Brunswick and Nova Scotia into the union because they saw there two wonderful seaports, namely, that of Saint John and the best seaport on the Atlantic coast, Halifax. After that, in 1873, my province was courted into this union as well. The royal commission, as set out at page 171 of the report, gives the terms of confederation. It says this:
Efficient steam service for the convenience of mails and passengers to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of the dominion, winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial Railway and the railway system of the dominion.
That is only part of the terms of confederation. That, to a certain extent, has been implemented in the last few years, by giving us certain daily communication by the different steamers we have had such as the Prince Edward, the Charlottetown and the Abegweit. But the royal commission should have gone a step further and given a full report of the agreement of 1873. For instance,

Supply-Transport
in addition to what I have already quoted, the following should have been added:
And such other charges as may be incident to and connected with the service which, by the British North America Act of 1867, appertain to the general government and as are or may be allowed to the other provinces.
That agreement was made some seventy years ago. Did the royal commission expect that Prince Edward Island would be satisfied with the conditions that existed seventy years ago, when one of the terms of union was supposed to have been equal transportation as appertains to the other provinces in the light of conditions as they changed from time to time? This is a question which it would take me too long to discuss tonight. However, there may be occasions later on when I can do so.
Another matter to which I should like to refer I have not been able to find in the report, but perhaps I have not been astute enough to get through it and to find the reference to it. The question is:	Who has the
right to set rates on ferry boats? This has always been a subject of contention and disagreement between myself and the smiling and genial Minister of Transport. However, I should like to find a suggestion from the royal commission as to who has that right.
When the excellent ship the Abegweit was turned over to the subcontractor of transportation, the Canadian National Railways, for purposes of operation, I raised the objection that she should not be turned over unless there was a proper agreement, and that agreement would be that the boat was to be operated under the terms of union of 1873.
This has been ignored entirely. When we joined confederation there were certain terms that have already been quoted. These are ignored by the subcontractors. I think it was still up to the government to see that we had a contract whereby, so far as Prince Edward Island was concerned, the boat would be operated according to the terms of confederation. However, that is another point upon which we can spend1 some time later.
Another matter with which I should like to deal is the Wood Island-Caribou ferry service. This is a system operated by Northumberland Ferries Limited, and it is one of the best transportation systems Prince Edward Island has. The company started in a small way, and the traffic has grown to the point where, today, they want larger boats for the accommodation of the service. I understand that a few days ago they presented a brief to the Minister of Transport and the government in this connection.
I do not think I should deal with the brief because I have no doubt that in connection

with it certain promises, which in a short time will be made public, have been made. I do want to say, however, that the minister should be very careful to fulfil all the recommendations in that brief. The company is deserving of the very best treatment from the government. It has given a good service; and had it not been for the ferry service we would have been entirely isolated from the mainland at the time of the railway strike. As it was we were isolated because, through the mistake of someone-I do not know who it was, nor do I want to blame anyone directly for it, until we have a final report- the car ferry was tied up. Here was a boat operating on the king's highway, as it is known in the terms of confederation. They had no right to go on strike; the government should have ordered them to continue or to get out. Then we would have had communication at least by car and truck.
However, before the strike was over the government, or someone, found out they were in error and the service was opened. Meantime the Wood Island ferry rendered a great service to the province. As I said a moment ago, I hope the Minister of Transport will take into consideration the brief presented to him on behalf of the Wood Island ferry, setting out what the company desires to do to give Prince Edward Island a better service. By doing so he will confer a great benefit on the province.
Then I would refer to another matter, namely another ferry service in the west end of the island. I know if the hon. member for Prince were here he certainly would be agitating for that ferry service. It is another link in our transportation system, if it could be got under way within the next year or so, and would be of great service to the farmers in the western part of the province.
Although my time is limited, there is one other matter I should like to mention. This has to do with the little question that comes up once in a while, namely the matter of maritime freight rates. Generally speaking, those who deal with this subject are led to believe that a subsidy is given to the maritime provinces under the provisions of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. However, when one looks into the matter he will see there is no subsidy. I cannot find where it has been dealt with in the report at all.
For instance, from 1912 to 1926 freight rates in the maritime provinces increased by 92 per cent. During the same time general freight rates across the rest of Canada had increased by only 55 per cent. After the Duncan commission made a study of this freight rate question as it concerned Prince Edward Island and the maritimes they

brought in a recommendation that there should be equalization of rates and 20 per cent was granted.
That was not a handout or a subsidy, it was simply a matter of equalizing freight rates with the rest of Canada. When we had been paying a 92 per cent increase as against a 55 per cent increase for the rest of Canada, even the 20 per cent did not give us proper equalization. What we should have is another 20 per cent to give us any preference at all on the importation of grains and our exports of potatoes.
These freight rates have always been referred to by a number of people as a subsidy, whereas, as I have tried to explain, it is not a subsidy at all. It was due us. We were only getting equalization with the rest of Canada.

I was sorely tempted to talk at greater length on the commission report, but inasmuch as we are close to eleven o'clock I shall take only a few minutes to discuss one matter I have in mind. Before the natural resources were turned over to the provinces a number of settlements were established in northern Alberta. One of these was Fort Vermilion, which was located along the Peace river about 200 miles from Peace River town. A little later on another settlement by the name of Carcajou was settled.
The only way these settlers had of getting into the settlements or going out with their products was by river boat. Fairly substantial farms were established and the whole country became quite a producer of grains and livestock, as the minister probably knows. Very early in the history of that northland the Hudson's Bay Company established boat and barge transportation to bring in their own merchandise and to carry out the furs and other products they obtained in their trading activities.
Not long ago a competitor started running boats and barges up and down the river
Supply-Transport
and continued in competition until last spring or summer. Civilization seemed to catch up with these people and then their troubles began. The rather rigid regulations governing river and marine transport were applied and this competitor to the Hudson's Bay Company could not continue operations. The main reason was the requirement that a qualified captain should be on the boats and that there should be proper passenger facilities even on boats that were carrying livestock. The Hudson's Bay Company did not increase their facilities. The result is that as late as August 1 last year close to 100,000 bushels of grain lay on the ground, covered with canvas or tarpaulins or whatever they could get, awaiting some form of transportation.
The situation became rather serious because the people could not market their livestock either. They are faced with an almost insurmountable problem because it takes quite a long time to build a road through that north country. There is no hope of a highway being built in time to serve this area. The new navigation season is about to begin and I was wondering if the minister could not bring to the attention of his departmental officers the necessity of looking into this matter to see if it would not be possible to relax the regulations and allow the private company to operate without having qualified captains and all these other things.
The men who have been operating up and down the river for 20 or 25 years know the river just as well as any captain could know it. They have never had any serious difficulty or any wrecks that resulted in loss of life or extensive property losses. That would seem to give assurance that by relaxing the regulations somewhat there would be no disaster. I ask the minister to look into the matter and see if he cannot help these people temporarily until such time as a better method of dealing with the problem can be found.
Yes, I will.
